title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
openingText: Somebody must have spread lies about Josef K.: one morning he was taken into custody, although he had done nothing wrong. His landlady, Mrs Grubach, employed a cook who brought him breakfast at roughly eight each morning; today she failed to appear. Nothing of the kind had ever happened. For a little while K. waited, watching from his pillow the old woman who lived across the way and was observing him with a curiosity quite foreign to her habits; then, puzzled and hungry together, he rang. A knock came at once, and in stepped somebody he had never encountered in this flat. Slim but solidly built, the man wore close-fitting black clothes furnished, rather like a travelling suit, with assorted pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons and a belt, which gave them an unusually serviceable appearance, though their particular purpose remained obscure. “Who might you be?” K. asked, already half sitting up. Ignoring the question, apparently expecting his presence to be accepted without inquiry, the man confined himself to asking: “Was it you who rang?” K. replied, “Anna is to bring me breakfast,” and for the time being tried to work out who this man actually was by silently observing him and thinking it over. But the stranger did not submit to scrutiny for long. Turning, he opened the door a fraction and told someone evidently just outside it: “He wants Anna to bring him breakfast.” A little laughter sounded from the adjoining room; one could not tell from its sound whether several people were laughing. Although this could have told the stranger nothing he had not known already, he now announced to K., as if delivering a report: “That cannot be done.” “That is a new development,” K. said, springing out of bed and hurriedly pulling on his trousers. “Let me see who these people next door are, and how Mrs Grubach proposes to answer for my being disturbed.” It immediately occurred to him that he need not have said this aloud, and that in saying it he had in a sense conceded the stranger's right to supervise him; just now, however, that scarcely seemed to matter. The stranger did take it that way, for he said: “Wouldn't staying here be better?” “I have no wish to stay here, or to be addressed by you until you have introduced yourself.” “I meant well,” the stranger said, opening the door now of his own accord. K. entered the adjoining room more slowly than he intended. At first sight it looked almost precisely as it had the previous evening. This was Mrs Grubach's sitting room; among its abundance of furniture, covers, china and photographs there was perhaps a little more space today than usual, but that was not immediately apparent, particularly since the chief alteration was a man seated with a book beside the open window, who now glanced up. “Your room was where you should have stayed! Didn't Franz tell you?” “Well, what is it you want?” K. asked, looking from this new acquaintance to the man called Franz, who had stopped in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window the old woman could be seen once more. With a truly aged person's inquisitiveness she had moved to the window now facing them so as to miss nothing. “I only want Mrs Grubach—” K. said, making a movement as if to break away from the two men, although neither was anywhere near him, and preparing to go on. “No,” said the one by the window, tossing his book onto a small table and getting up. “Leaving is not permitted. You are in custody, after all.” “So it would appear,” K. replied; then he asked: “And on what grounds?” “Explaining that is outside our assignment. Return to your room and wait there. Proceedings have been set in motion, and in due course you will be informed of everything. In speaking to you so kindly I am already exceeding my instructions. Still, I hope nobody but Franz can hear me, and he too is treating you kindly against every regulation. If your luck holds as well as it did when your guards were chosen, you have grounds for confidence.” K. wanted to sit, but now discovered that the armchair at the window was the only seat anywhere in the room. “You'll come to recognise the truth of all this,” Franz said, approaching him together with the other man. That second man in particular towered well above K. and repeatedly patted his shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt. They said he would now have to put on a far inferior shirt, but that they would keep this one, together with his other linen, and restore it to him if his business turned out favourably. “Better to entrust your belongings to us than to the store,” they said, “because things are often misappropriated there; besides, once a certain time has passed everything is sold, whether the proceedings concerned have ended or not. And cases of this sort go on for so long, especially lately. You would eventually receive the proceeds from the store, of course, but in the first place the proceeds are small to begin with: a sale is decided by the size of the bribe, not the size of the bid; and experience shows that sums like these shrink further as they are passed from one hand to another and carried over year after year.” K. scarcely attended to their speeches. Whatever control over his possessions he might still retain meant little to him; what mattered much more was getting a clear understanding of his situation. In these people's presence he could not even think. The second guard's belly—for guards were the only thing they could be—kept bumping him, almost companionably; yet whenever he raised his eyes he saw, wholly at odds with this fat body, a lean, bony face with a prominent nose turned sideways, communicating over his head with the other guard. Who could these people be? What were they talking about? Which authority employed them? Surely he lived under the rule of law; peace prevailed everywhere, every statute remained in force; who dared invade his lodgings? His usual inclination was to take things as lightly as possible, to believe in the worst only once it had happened, and to make no provision for the future even when everything looked threatening. Here that did not seem right. Certainly the whole affair could be viewed as a joke, a crude practical joke arranged by his fellow bank employees for some unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday. That was possible, naturally; perhaps he need only laugh in the guards' faces somehow and they would join in, perhaps they were porters from the street corner, whom they rather resembled—nevertheless, on this occasion, virtually from his first sight of the guard Franz, he had resolved to surrender not the slightest advantage he might possess over these people. That he might later be accused of failing to appreciate a joke struck K. as a very small danger. But he recalled—though learning from experience was otherwise no habit of his—a few incidents, insignificant in themselves, in which he had deliberately behaved incautiously, unlike his friends, without the faintest sense of the possible consequences, and the outcome had punished him for it. That must not recur, at least on this occasion; if this was a comedy, he would take his part.
about:
Josef K. wakes to find strangers taking charge of his room and his breakfast. They say he is under arrest, but let him go to work. No one tells him what he has done. His efforts to obtain an explanation draw him into hearings, offices and conversations in which every apparent source of help creates another uncertainty.

Kafka gives this extraordinary situation the texture of ordinary life: a missed breakfast, a crowded staircase, a neighbour disturbed at night, the pressure of work at a bank. K. argues, calculates and defends his standing. The narration stays close to him without settling whether his understanding of other people is reliable. The unease often arrives through comedy.

Written in 1914–1915 and left unfinished, the novel first appeared in 1925 in an edition arranged by Max Brod. This package follows the ten main chapters in a transcription of that first edition and uses neutral numbered labels. Its modern English is a fresh Tinct rendering directly from the German; there is no human English translation supplied as a comparison edition.

whyItMatters.title: An accusation without an explanation
whyItMatters.body: K. is expected to respond before he knows what he must answer. The novel makes that imbalance concrete through appointments, rooms and conversations, asking what a defence can mean when the terms of judgment remain unavailable.

whyItMatters.title: The authority we help to sustain
whyItMatters.body: K. resists the court, yet seeks its recognition, follows its leads and measures other people by their influence. His changing conduct lets readers examine how opposition and dependence can grow together.

whyItMatters.title: A voice that leaves judgment open
whyItMatters.body: The narration reports absurd arrangements with practical precision. It also follows K.’s quick conclusions closely enough to make them persuasive without guaranteeing that they are true. Reading means noticing the distance between what happens and what he believes it means.

angleCards.title: Who knows what?
angleCards.text: Track each claim about the court back to its speaker. Which claims rest on observation, which on hearsay, and which on K.’s own interpretation?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish events from claims about them and notice when an assumption starts being treated as knowledge.

angleCards.title: The comedy of procedure
angleCards.text: Watch the breakfast, clothing, furniture and timing. How do practical inconveniences make official power both ridiculous and effective?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the dry comedy of ordinary objects and routines without losing sight of the coercion they carry.

angleCards.title: Doors, rooms and permission
angleCards.text: Notice who may enter a room, who has to wait, and who listens from outside. The novel repeatedly turns access to private and public space into a question of authority.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track thresholds and intrusions, including K.’s own treatment of other people’s boundaries.

angleCards.title: Reading an unfinished novel
angleCards.text: The ten-chapter sequence comes through Brod’s posthumous arrangement. Read the connections carefully while leaving room for breaks, uncertainties and questions the novel does not settle.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how the arranged sequence shapes my expectations without treating every unresolved detail as a puzzle with one final answer.

cast.name: Josef K.
cast.description: A senior bank employee who expects reason, status and professional competence to make his position clear. An unexplained arrest draws those expectations into question.

cast.name: Mrs Grubach
cast.description: K.’s landlady, whose concern for her lodgers includes close attention to their reputations. Her domestic judgments accompany the first official intrusion.

cast.name: Miss Bürstner
cast.description: A typist whose room is used during K.’s arrest. She listens to his account while insisting on her own time, space and responsibility.

cast.name: Franz and Willem
cast.description: The two men who take charge of K. on the morning of his arrest. They invoke regulations while making their own demands.

cast.name: The examining magistrate
cast.role: The official at the first hearing
cast.description: He presides over the crowded room where K. tries to turn his examination into a public challenge to the proceedings.

cast.name: K.’s uncle
cast.description: A relative from the country who takes an urgent interest in K.’s case and introduces him to a lawyer.

cast.name: Huld
cast.description: A lawyer approached through K.’s uncle. His account of defence work raises questions about access, influence and dependence.

cast.name: Leni
cast.description: A woman in the lawyer’s household who takes a close personal interest in K.

cast.name: Titorelli
cast.description: A painter with connections to the court, approached as a possible source of help.

cast.name: Block
cast.description: A merchant whose experience of the proceedings gives K. another perspective on seeking legal assistance.

cast.name: The priest
cast.description: A clergyman whose conversation with K. turns on how a story about access to the law can be understood.
